'''Kamo Shrine''' (鴨神社) is a [[Setsumatsusha|sessha]] of [[Kōtai Jingū]] ([[Ise Grand Shrine]]) (Inner Shrine). It is located on the mid-slope of [[Mount Dainichi]], and is considered the most challenging [[Shinto shrine]] to reach among the [[List of Shikinaisha in Ise Province|125 Shrines of Ise]]<ref name="gk">[[Gakken Plus Co., Ltd.]] (2013): p.69</ref>.

== Overview ==
[[Kamo shrines|Kamo Shrine]] is located at 1398 Okatani, Yamaga, Tamaki Town, Watarai District, Mie Prefecture<ref name="sk1">Shikinaisha Kenkyūkai (1990): p.201</ref>. It is one of the 13 auxiliary and subordinate shrines of the [[Kōtai Jingū]] (Inner Shrine) located in Tamaki Town and Ranks 4th among the 27 auxiliary shrines of the Inner Shrine<ref>Ujiyamada City Hall (1929): pp.9–11</ref>.

The "Kamo" in the shrine name was traditionally believed to refer to an old place name. However, archaeological progress at the [[Saikū]] site has led to suggestions of a connection with the [[Kamo clan]], who served as water administrators<ref name="sk9">Shikinaisha Kenkyūkai (1990): p.199</ref>.

The shrine grounds cover an area of 15,018 m²<ref name="sk2">Shikinaisha Kenkyūkai (1990): p.202</ref>. The shrine building is constructed in the [[Shinmei-zukuri]] style with a wooden plank roof, facing south, and is enclosed by a single layer of [[Sacred fences|Tamagaki]]<ref name="sk2"/>. It features one [[Torii]]<ref name="sk2"/>. The sacred object (shintai) is a stone<ref>Kaneko (1983): p.59</ref>. There is no offertory box.

A stream flowing beneath the shrine grounds is said to have never dried up, even during droughts<ref name="ic">Ise Bunka-sha (2008): p.65</ref>. The trees on the grounds display beautiful autumn foliage during late autumn<ref name="ic"/>.

== Enshrined Deities ==
The enshrined deities are '''Ishikorowake no Mikoto''' (石己呂和居命) and '''Mimae no Kami''' (御前神)<ref name="gk"/><ref name="ic"/>. Both deities are children of [[Ōminakami no Mikoto]] and are considered gods of agriculture and irrigation<ref name="gk"/><ref name="ic"/>. Originally, there were separate shrine buildings for each deity<ref name="uy">Ujiyamada City Hall (1929): p.10</ref>, but after the shrine was restored by [[Kawabe Masanaga]] during the Edo period, the deities have been enshrined together in a single structure<ref name="sk2"/>.

== History ==
According to the ''Enryaku Gishiki-chō'', the shrine was established during the reign of [[Yamatohime-no-mikoto]]<ref>Kaneko (1983): p.68</ref>, giving it a history as long as the Ise Grand Shrine itself<ref name="sk0">Shikinaisha Kenkyūkai (1990): p.200</ref>. In ancient texts, the shrine is referred to as "Kamo-sha" or "Kamo Jinja," and its reading as "Kamo" is undisputed<ref name="sk9"/>.

It was designated to undergo reconstruction every 20 years, following the tradition of the [[Jingū Shikinen Sengū|Shikinen Sengū]] at the Ise Grand Shrine<ref name="sk0"/>. However, records of reconstruction ceased after an entry from December 8, 1340, which mentions an order to rebuild the shrine using rice tributes from Tajima Province<ref name="sk0"/>.

In 1663 (Kanbun 3), the shrine was restored by Grand Priest [[Kawabe Masanaga]] in Yamaga Village, Okatani<ref name="sk0"/>. [[Mikannagi Kiyonao]] later criticized this restoration site as inappropriate in his work ''Ninomiya Kansha Engaku Kō'', proposing that the original site was within Yamaga Village at the remains of the former [[Yahashira Shrine]], which had been merged in 1908 (Meiji 41)<ref>Shikinaisha Kenkyūkai (1990): pp.201–202</ref>.

The current location was established in 1876 (Meiji 9)<ref name="sk0"/>. The shrine building was reconstructed in 1922 (Taishō 11)<ref name="uy"/>.

== Rituals ==
On the 16th day of the 3rd lunar month, a ritual known as ''Miyatamori Shinji'' (宮田もり神事) is held, which is associated with [[Kōshin|Kōshin belief]]<ref>Sakurai (1991): p.293</ref>.

During the [[Kinensai|Kinen-sai]] (February), [[Tsukinami-sai]] (June and December), [[Kannamesai Festival|Kannamesai]] (October), and [[Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niiname-sai]] (November), rituals are conducted in front of the shrine. For the [[Saitan-sai]] (January 1), [[Genshi-sai]] (January), [[Kenkoku Kinen no Hi]] (February 11), [[Kazahi-no-Misai]] (May and August), and [[The Emperor's Birthday]] (December 23), remote rituals are performed at the Gojōden of the Ise Grand Shrine<ref>Shikinaisha Kenkyūkai (1990): pp.200–201</ref>.

== Access ==
Near the shrine are the ruins of an ancient icehouse (氷室) associated with the [[Saikū]]<ref name="ic"/>. About 2.5 km from Kamo Shrine is the [[Kamoshimo Shrine]], which enshrines the same deity and is located within the same Shirota region<ref name="sk0"/>.

; By Public Transport
There are no nearby train stations or bus stops. From [[Tamaru Station]] on the [[Sangū Line|JR Sangū Line]], it is about a 50-minute walk (4.0 km) southwest, or about 53 minutes (4.3 km) south from [[Tokida Station|Sotojōda Station]]<ref name="ic"/>. From Yamaga village, a stone marker labeled "Kamo Shrine" leads through a bamboo grove, under a tunnel beneath the [[Ise Expressway]], and along a mountain path to the shrine<ref name="ic"/>. The distance from the marker to the shrine is about 1.1 km<ref>Ise Bunka-sha (2008): p.63</ref>, taking around 20 minutes<ref name="gk"/>. There are forestry roads nearby, so caution is advised to avoid getting lost<ref name="ic"/>.

; By Car
From [[Tamaki interchange]] on the Ise Expressway, it takes about 6 minutes (2.1 km) to reach the stone marker for Kamo Shrine<ref name="gk"/>. The mountain path beyond the marker is for pedestrians only, and vehicles cannot pass through. However, there is a parking area near [[Matoyama Park]], which is accessible via a tunnel under the Ise Expressway. This route includes a paved mountain path, reducing the walking distance.
